newsitem.title: CROATIA: Radio clampdown sparks protests in Croatia.
newsitem.headline: Radio clampdown sparks protests in Croatia.

text.p: Croatia faced mounting international criticism on Thursday of its bid to close an influential independent radio station, while domestic opposition grew into a wider demand for more democracy.

The United States and Britain sharply criticised the Zagreb government's move against Radio 101. In Croatia itself, a prominent human rights activist called for a mass street demonstration in the capital.

Ivan Zvonimir Cicak, head of the Croatian branch of the human rights watchdog Helsinki Committee (HHO), called on the radio's listeners and all "free-minded people" to gather at Zagreb's main square on Thursday night in support of Radio 101.

In a statement broadcast on the radio, the HHO urged people to gather in the central Ban Jelacic square and light candles, recalling the peaceful protests that brought down communism in Croatia in late 1989 and early 1990.
"Use the candle flames to light the path of democracy in Croatia," Cicak said in a live broadcast.
Croatia's rightist government moved on Wednesday to shut down the popular independent local radio station. Radio 101 lost a licence review over its programming and for "legal reasons".
The state-controlled Telecommunications Council announced it had awarded Radio 101's frequency to a non-existent rival station whose owner has close links with the ruling party.
The decision caused an avalanche of protests and expressions of support from public figures, including ruling party members, soldiers and Zagreb residents.
The station aired telegrams of support late into the night and on Thursday morning, when the national telephone service complained that it had been flooded with calls.
Radio 101, founded in 1984, was one of the prime promoters of the peaceful changes that led to the country's first democratic elections in April 1990.

President Franjo Tudjman won the poll and led the nation to bloody secession from Yugoslavia. Since then he has been criticised for ruling the country with an authoritarian hand, clamping down on political opponents and independent media.
"The political atmosphere in Zagreb now is similar to that in 1989," independent commentator Davor Gjenero said.
"There is a lot of frustration against the authoritarian or totalitarian type of government. The Radio 101 is just a symbol," Gjenero told Reuters.
Croatian citizens were not the only ones concerned by the closure.
"This development in the case of Radio 101 constitues a significant setback for democratisation and free expression in Croatia," said a U.S. state department spokesman.

"Unless the Government of Croatia acts quickly to assign Radio 101 another comparable frequency, this decision by the Broadcasting Council will mean the loss of a principal voice of independent news and opposition viewpopints in Croatia," said state department spokesman Glyn Davies.
The British Foreign Office also said it was concerned about the closure and urged Croatian authorities to reconsider.
There was no official government reaction but some members of the ruling Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ), including several government ministers, washed their hands of the decision.
"As a Deputy Prime Minister, I will support (the motion) for Radio 101 to continue broadcasting," Minister Borislav Skegro told the radio.
Most state-controlled dailies had front page coverage of Wednesday's events with pictures of public protests.
President Tudjman, who has been receiving treatment at a U.S. military hospital near Washington, was due to return to Croatia on Friday, according to his private doctor.
